Lal Kitab reads this as a life of earning results through action and remedy, not inheriting them easily. Lal Kitab exaltation and debilitation houses: none occupied Calculated . 26.4.2 Planet by planet: placement first, then hidden strength, then net verdict Jupiter, H1 (retrograde, with Ketu). Placement: Lal Kitab's Jupiter in the 1st is a king's position, respected like a guru, but its fortune is tied to self-earned standing. Hidden strength: in Lal Kitab Jupiter disciplines Ketu (the "guru with the dog"), so Ketu's restlessness is harnessed. A masnui Jupiter in H8 doubles the planet. Net: strong . What this means for you: dignity, counsel and a teacher's role come naturally. Keep your word and the chart's best planet stays bright. Ketu, H1. Placement: travel, sons and restlessness at the self. Hidden: tamed by Jupiter, but it triggers Bhai rin and Kudrati rin. Net: mixed, managed . What this means for you: a mobile life (Pennsylvania to North Carolina is already one move). Dogs are your Ketu remedy. Saturn, H3 (retrograde, Ashwini). Placement: Lal Kitab treats Saturn in the 3rd as protective: watchful eyes and the house guarded. Hidden: retrograde, sitting in a horse nakshatra. Net: good . What this means for you: steady courage and protective siblings or cousins. Stay away from acting on others' quarrels. Moon, H6. Placement: a Moon among enemies. It gives service, mediation and maternal-side ties. Hidden: it triggers Behen rin and Kudrati rin. Net: weak, fixable . What this means for you: you serve best when you serve quietly. Keep silver and milk-related charity simple (the cowrie remedy below). Mars, H7 (with Rahu). Placement: Mars in the partnership house brings forceful partnerships and business drive. Hidden: this is your maturity planet now (Mars matures at 28) and the 35-year cycle also points to H7. Net: active, needs restraint . What this means for you: the years 26–33 put partnerships and contracts in the spotlight, more than any other part of the chart. Rahu, H7. Placement: sudden or unconventional partnerships. Hidden: triggers Stri rin. Net: mixed . What this means for you: take time choosing partners. The traditional remedy is to feed cows. Sun, H8 (with Venus). Placement: Sun in the hidden house works behind the scenes and gains from others' resources. Hidden: Sun and Venus combine into a masnui Jupiter. Net: hidden-strong . What this means for you: your strength is unseen and grows through research, joint funds and inheritance-type matters. Venus, H8. Placement: Lal Kitab is uneasy about Venus in the 8th for the spouse's ease. Hidden: part of the masnui Jupiter. Net: mixed, redeemed . What this means for you: the protective formula is respect in marriage. Mercury, H9. Placement: intelligent, religious-minded and well travelled, but in the father's house it triggers Pitri rin. Net: good, with a debt . What this means for you: learning and pilgrimage suit you. Honour the elders on your father's side. 26.4.3 Aspects, sleeping houses and teva type Calculated Lal Kitab "takkar" aspects: 1→7 (Jupiter/Ketu meet Mars/Rahu head-on), 3→9 and 3→11 (Saturn to Mercury), 2→6 (empty H2 → Moon) and 8→2 (Sun/Venus to an empty H2). Sleeping houses: H4, H5, H10, H12. The teva is not nabalig and not andha (blind). Takkar aspects Conditions What this means for you: the main axis is H1 against H7: self against partner, Jupiter's wisdom against Mars's force. Ifá isn't something you can calculate. It is a divination system. A babaláwo (an Ifá priest) casts a sign with sixteen palm nuts (ìkín) or a divining chain (ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀), with the client present, and then recites verses. Nobody can work out a person's real birth Odù from a date. So this chapter does two separate things, and I keep them apart throughout: Everything the calendar and sky really give. These are the weekday, the Yoruba four-day week, the Kọ́jọ́dá date, the Akan soul-day name, the Akan 42-day cycle, the Dogon Sigui position, and the sky over Johnstown at your birth. These items are actually computed. A constructed cast. This is a fixed, repeatable stand-in for the cast a babaláwo would make. It comes from the SHA-256 hash of the string 1998-10-13T21:25Z|40.33N|78.92W|M . The first eight bits give the two legs of the chain, and the later bits give the ìbò, the cowrie cast and the kola cast. Every result from it is labelled CONSTRUCTED. It shows how the system works using your own data. It does not replace a real itá. The full checklist of items is in deep/27_ifa_inventory.md . The code is in deep/27/compute.py and the results are in deep/27/result.json .

1. The sixteen principal Odù The 16 principal Odù Ifá has sixteen "mother" signs, called Ojú Odù or Méjì. In the usual seniority order they are Ogbè, Ọ̀yẹ̀kú, Ìwòrì, Òdí, Ìrosùn, Ọ̀wọ́nrín, Ọ̀bàrà, Ọ̀kànràn, Ògúndá, Ọ̀sá, Ìká, Òtúúrúpọ̀n, Òtúrá, Ìrẹtẹ̀, Ọ̀ṣẹ́ and Òfún (Abimbọ́la, Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus , 1976; Bascom, Ifa Divination , 1969). Each one is a column of four marks. A single stroke (I) is one mark and a double stroke (II) is two. Ogbè is all single, light and open. Ọ̀yẹ̀kú is all double, night and closed. What this means for you: both halves of your constructed sign come from the first five, the most senior group. Ọ̀yẹ̀kú is second in rank and Ìrosùn is fifth. In Ifá thinking, seniority means weight and age, not luck. Your sign is made of old material. 2. The 256 Odù The 256 matrix When two different principal Odù appear on the right and left legs, the result is one of 240 "child" signs (Ọmọ Odù or Àmúlù). Together with the 16 Méjì, that makes 16 × 16 = 256. The sign is named right leg first. Each of the 256 has its own body of ẹsẹ̀ (verses) (Abimbọ́la 1976; Bascom 1969). The cell number in the figure is just a row-by-row index. The seniority order of the 240 differs from lineage to lineage. What this means for you: your constructed sign is Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ìrosùn (cell 21). It is a child sign, not a Méjì. A child sign is read as the right Odù acting through the left one. So for you that is night, ancestors and endings, working through memory, lineage and red camwood. 3. The constructed cast Constructed cast His sign, large On a real ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀ chain, each leg has four half-seed pods. Concave side up gives one mark and convex up gives two (Bascom 1969). Here bits 1–4 of the hash gave 2 2 2 2 = Ọ̀yẹ̀kú on the right and bits 5–8 gave 1 1 2 2 = Ìrosùn on the left. What this means for you: Ọ̀yẹ̀kú means the closing of the day, the ancestors, and what has to be honoured before anything new can start. Ìrosùn is tied to ọsùn (red camwood powder) and to remembering. In practice its verses often deal with the family line and with keeping a name alive. Put together, the sign describes someone who moves forward by honouring what came before, whose success is a kind of remembering. 4. Ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀ and ìkín: two ways to the same sign Ìkín is the more senior method. The babaláwo holds the sixteen nuts and tries to grab them all in one hand. If one nut is left over he marks II. If two are left he marks I. Any other result doesn't count and he grabs again. He repeats this eight times. The ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀ gives all eight marks in a single throw (Bascom 1969). Both methods produce the same 256 signs. What this means for you: the constructed cast imitates the ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀, the quick daily method. A birth or initiation reading would normally use ìkín. That is one more reason to treat the constructed sign as a sketch. 5. Ọpọ́n Ifá, the tray Ọpọ́n with his marks drawn in the powder The marks are drawn with a finger in ìyẹ̀rọ̀sùn, the powdered wood dust spread on the ọpọ́n. The carved face on the rim is Èṣù, the messenger who carries the sign between people and the gods (Abimbọ́la 1976). The image above shows Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ìrosùn drawn into the powder with PIL. What this means for you: the sign sits under Èṣù's eye. In Ifá no reading counts until Èṣù has carried it, which is why ẹbọ (offering) always includes his share. 6. Ìbò, the determinant Ìbò After the sign comes out, the babaláwo asks yes/no questions using paired objects held in the client's hands, such as a cowrie (yes) and a bone (no). The first question is whether the sign comes with ire (good fortune) or ibi (misfortune). Then he narrows down which kind of ire: long life, money, a spouse, children, ìṣẹ́gun (victory) and so on. The constructed ìbò came out ire , kind ire ìṣẹ́gun, victory over opposition . What this means for you: ire ìṣẹ́gun is the "your road opens against resistance" answer. It doesn't promise there will be no opposition. It assumes there will be, and promises you come through. 7. Ẹsẹ̀ Ifá: the verses of Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ìrosùn Ifá verses follow a fixed pattern. A priest's name, a client's problem, the prescribed ẹbọ, the result, and a closing song. For this sign, published practitioner commentaries (for example the openifa / ifa-wisdom pages for Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ìrosùn) stress the client's line and ancestors and patience before results. Their passages about bodily illness are left out here on purpose, because this book has a rule against health content. I don't quote any verse text that I couldn't check against a published corpus. What this means for you: the recurring advice is to make your forebears part of your plans. That can be as simple as telling their story and carrying their name forward. 8. Èèwọ̀ (taboos) and ẹbọ (offerings) Each Odù brings èèwọ̀ and an ẹbọ, but only the casting priest assigns them, based on the ìbò answers (Bascom 1969). None are invented here. What this means for you: if you ever go for a real reading, the taboos you're given will come from that reading, not from this chapter. 9. Mẹ́rìndínlógún (sixteen cowries) Cowries Priests of the òrìṣà, rather than babaláwo, throw sixteen cowries and count the number that land mouth up. Each count from 1 to 16 is an odù. Seven is Òdí (Bascom, Sixteen Cowries , 1980). The constructed throw gave 7. What this means for you: in cowrie divination Òdí is a sign about something hidden or closed that has to be brought out properly. That fits with your Ifá halves, night and memory. 10. Obì (kola) Kola Four kola lobes are thrown. Three up and one down is Ìtagbà (Ẹtawa in some places), which means "yes, but confirm it." The constructed cast gave Ìtagbà. The names for each result vary by region (Bascom 1969). What this means for you: this is a yes that asks for a second step. It agrees with ire ìṣẹ́gun: the result is good, but you have to follow it up. Synthesis of Part I: all four constructed casts point the same way. Ifá gives Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ìrosùn with ire ìṣẹ́gun. The cowries give Òdí, the hidden thing brought out. The kola gives a yes that needs confirming. The picture is of a person whose progress comes from honouring lineage and ancestors and from meeting resistance, and whose rewards come in a second movement rather than the first.

Ẹsẹ̀ntáyé (Àkọsẹ̀jáyé): the sign "of the feet" Ẹsẹ̀ntáyé with marks On the third day after a birth, a babaláwo places the baby's feet on the ọpọ́n, or presents the child to Ifá, and casts the sign that the child "stepped into the world" with. That sign guides how the child is raised and named, and what taboos apply (jolan.com.ng; ondestinyspath.com 2018; see the practitioner essay at JSTOR 10.2307/1145850). Your ẹsẹ̀ntáyé was never cast. The constructed sign stands in for it. What this means for you: if the constructed sign had been your real ẹsẹ̀ntáyé, a family following custom would have taught you your lineage history early on, because Ìrosùn's theme is memory. 12. The naming day The naming ceremony (ìsọmọlórúkọ) traditionally takes place on the 7th day for girls and the 9th for boys, with the 8th for twins in many towns. Some names come straight from Ifá: Fálọ́lá, Ifáṣeun, Awóyẹmí. A name with "Ifá" or "Awo" in it can mark a child whose sign or birth day belongs to Ifá. What this means for you: because you were born on the Ifá day (§16), a traditional family could have given you an Ifá-root name. In Yoruba terms your birthday already carries that. 13. Ìtẹ̀fá and the itá Ìtẹ̀fá is initiation into Ifá. During it the initiate's personal Odù (Odù Ifá) is cast, and on the third day there is an itá, a full reading of that person's life (Abimbọ́la 1976; Maupoil 1943 for the Fon parallel). That is the only real "birth chart" in Ifá, and you can't compute it. What this means for you: this is the main gap in the chapter, and it can only be filled by a living priest. 14. Odù Ọdún, the sign of the year Every year many communities and temples cast an Odù for the coming year at the Ifá festival. I couldn't find a published Odù Ọdún for the year 1998–99 that I could check. This is stated as a gap. 15. Ilà (facial marks) Ilà show which lineage and town a person belongs to. They don't come from the birth sign. Portraits: no Odù verse, Fá text, Akan day-name lore or Dogon source describes the face of a person born under a particular sign or day. No tradition gives a face for you. The portrait-style artwork below is atmosphere only. Synthesis of Part II: the customs around birth (the third-day reading, the naming day, the itá) are exactly the things that can't be done by calculation. What carries over is the pattern. A child's sign is meant to be read out loud and turned into a name and a set of rules. Your calendar items, especially the Ifá day, are the closest thing you have to that.

16. The Yoruba four-day week (ọ̀sẹ̀) Four-day week The traditional Yoruba week has four days, each sacred to a deity. Under the Kọ́jọ́dá convention the order is Ọjọ́ Ọbàtálá, Ọjọ́ Ṣàngó (Jàkúta), Ọjọ́ Ọ̀rúnmìlà (Ọjọ́ Awo, Ifá's day) and Ọjọ́ Ògún. Markets in many towns run on this cycle (Wikipedia "Yoruba calendar"; NACAPA Kọ́jọ́dá; ipilese.com). Counting from the published anchor (1 June 2011 = Ọjọ́ Ọbàtálá), 13 October 1998 falls on Ọjọ́ Ọ̀rúnmìlà, the day of Ifá itself. The Ìpìlẹ̀ṣẹ̀ texts point out that the day order and starting point vary from town to town, so this is the result under the Kọ́jọ́dá convention. What this means for you: this is the strongest calendar item in the chapter. You were born on the day set aside for Ọ̀rúnmìlà, the witness of destiny, the same god whose system this chapter is about. In Yoruba terms that's a birth inside the house of wisdom and divination. 17. The Kọ́jọ́dá date Kọ́jọ́dá Kọ́jọ́dá is a modern standardised version of the calendar. The year starts on 3 June, the count begins at 1958 = 10000, and each month has 28 days (seven four-day weeks). Under it your birth is year 10040, month 5, day 21 . The Gregorian-aligned name for October is Ọ̀wàrà , the month of heavy rains and storms (Wikipedia; NACAPA). The Ìpìlẹ̀ṣẹ̀ material warns that the fixed new year and the 10,000-year count are 20th-century reconstructions. What this means for you: day 21 of a 28-day month opens the last week of the month. You arrived in the closing stretch, which echoes Ọ̀yẹ̀kú's theme of endings. Ọ̀wàrà, the storm month, matches ire ìṣẹ́gun's victory through turbulence. 18. The Moon (Òṣùpá) at birth The Moon was a waning crescent, 35% lit, below the Johnstown horizon. The previous new moon was 20 September and the next full moon 4 November 1998 (ephem). Yoruba months were traditionally counted from one new crescent to the next (Wikipedia). What this means for you: you were born in the dark, closing half of the moon's month, another Ọ̀yẹ̀kú-coloured signal. 19. Market cycles Because markets follow the four-day week, a day sacred to Ọ̀rúnmìlà is also a particular market day in towns that keep this cycle. What this means for you: traditionally your birth day would have been a day of exchange and consultation, with people seeing a diviner before trading. Synthesis of Part III: the calendar gives you the Ifá day, a late-month date in the storm month, and a waning moon. All three lean the same way as the constructed sign: wisdom, closing and inheritance, and coming through turbulence.

Orí diagram 20. Orí inú and Orí òde Orí is the "inner head", your personal divinity of destiny. Orí òde is the physical head. Ifá teaches that no òrìṣà can help a person their Orí does not support (Abimbọ́la 1976; Akanmidu, PhilArchive AKATIA). What this means for you: in Yoruba terms the first thing to look after is your own Orí, through good character and attention to yourself, before asking any god for anything. 21. The three ways destiny is taken Àkúnlẹ̀yàn is what you knelt and chose in heaven. Àkúnlẹ̀gbà is what you knelt and were given. Àyànmọ́ is what is fixed and comes with you (PhilArchive AKATIA; american-ifa.com). What this means for you: part of your path is your own choice, part was handed to you, and part is fixed. Ifá treats the first two as open to influence through ẹbọ and character. 22. Àjàlá and the three friends In the story, Afúwàpẹ́, Orìṣẹ̀ẹ̀kú and Orílẹ̀mẹ̀rẹ̀ go to Àjàlá, the potter who moulds heads. Only Afúwàpẹ́ consults Ifá first and chooses a good Orí. The other two pick heads that look fine but crack (Abimbọ́la 1976). What this means for you: you were born on Ifá's day. That's the calendar version of Afúwàpẹ́'s choice to consult first. 23. Ìwà (character) Ìwà pẹ̀lẹ́, gentle character, is called the true partner of Orí. Ifá verses describe Ìwà as Ọ̀rúnmìlà's wife, who leaves him when she is treated badly (Abimbọ́la 1976). What this means for you: whatever any sign says, character is the part of your destiny you can steer. 24. Ẹlẹ́rìí-ìpín Ọ̀rúnmìlà is called Ẹlẹ́rìí-ìpín, "witness of the choosing of destiny", because he was present when every Orí was chosen (ipilese.com; Abimbọ́la 1976). What this means for you: you were born on the witness's own day. In this framework that's the closest thing to having your choice witnessed. Synthesis of Part IV: Orí teaching puts responsibility on the person. Your calendar items put you in Ifá's domain, and the constructed sign adds lineage and ancestors. Taken together they describe a destiny that grows by consulting, remembering and keeping good character.

I found no reliable Yoruba names for these planets, so they are given their English names. What this means for you: Jupiter was coming up at the moment you were born. It's the only body crossing the horizon, rising as the Sun goes down. 33. Ìràwọ̀, ìràwọ̀ onírù, Òṣùmàrè Ìràwọ̀ means star, ìràwọ̀ onírù means comet (the "star with a tail"), and Òṣùmàrè is the rainbow serpent-deity (yoruba-scipedia). What this means for you: no comet or rainbow is tied to your date. Òṣùmàrè appears in the art below as the bridge between sky and earth. 34. Sirius, the Pleiades and Orion: a gap Sirius was 62° below the horizon. Some web sources give Yoruba names for these stars, but I couldn't find any reliable attestation for them, so none are given here. Synthesis of Part VI: the sky backs up the rest of the chapter. A late Sun, a hidden Venus, an absent Moon and a rising Jupiter make a closing-day, hidden-light birth with something rising at the horizon.

Fon Fá names 35. The sixteen Fá du Gbe, Yeku, Woli, Di, Loso, Wlen, Abla, Akla, Guda, Sa, Ka, Trukpen, Tula, Lete, Ce, Fu. That gives 256 signs (Maupoil, La Géomancie à l'ancienne Côte des Esclaves , 1943). What this means for you: your constructed sign in Fá is Yeku-Loso . 36. Kpoli, the personal sign In Fá a person receives their personal sign, the Kpoli, at initiation (Fá-sɛ). It is linked to a person's sɛ (destiny) and is guarded by Legba (Maupoil 1943). It can't be computed. What this means for you: this is the same kind of gap as the Yoruba itá. 37. Legba Legba is Fá's messenger, the equivalent of Èṣù. What this means for you: in both traditions your sign passes through the doorkeeper first. Synthesis of Part VII: Fá confirms the Yoruba structure. The same sixteen roots and the same 256 signs mean Yeku-Loso is the same reading in a neighbouring language.

Akan kra din 38. Kra din: Kwabena An Akan child is first named for the day of birth. A Tuesday-born boy is Kwabena (Kobena, Ebo, Kwabla), and his day-soul is Bena (learnakan.com; UNC Teaching Africa Akan naming lesson). Christaller (1933) explains the kra-din as the soul-name: the kra (soul) takes its destiny (nkrabea) from Onyame on that day. What this means for you: your Akan name is Kwabena. 39. Bena and the ocean The UNC lesson links Tuesday with the ocean (Ɛpo / Bosompo). What this means for you: your soul-day is the ocean's day: depth, a horizon, and things moving underneath. It pairs naturally with Ọ̀yẹ̀kú's night. 40. Kra, sunsum, ntoro, mogya The kra is the life-soul from Onyame. Sunsum is personality, linked to the father's ntoro . Mogya is the blood of the mother's abusua (clan) (Christaller; Rattray). What this means for you: your Akan profile puts the ocean-day soul at the centre, with lineage on both sides. Again that matches Ìrosùn. 41. Nkrabea and Orí Nkrabea is the Akan counterpart of àyànmọ́. Both are a destiny taken before birth. What this means for you: two neighbouring traditions agree that you came with a destiny already taken. 42. Adaduanan, the 42-day cycle Adaduanan The Akan ritual calendar runs on a 42-day cycle (6 × 7) anchored to Akwasidae, a Sunday festival. Counting back from the published Akwasidae of 11 October 2026 (Manhyia Palace; nyamedua.org), your birth fell 23 days after an Akwasidae , on day 24 of its cycle. That is between Awukudae and the next Akwasidae. What this means for you: you were born in an ordinary working stretch, not on a festival. That fits a destiny built by work. Synthesis of Part VIII: Kwabena, the ocean, and a soul whose destiny was taken from Onyame. The Akan system supports both Orí theory and the sign's lineage theme.

Sigui timeline 43. Sirius and the Griaule question Marcel Griaule and Germaine Dieterlen claimed the Dogon knew Sirius was a double star (po tolo / sigu tolo). Walter van Beek's restudy ( Current Anthropology 32(2), 1991, 139–167) found that the Dogon call Sirius dana tolo , "the hunter's star", and that no informant knew of Sirius as a double. See also Ortiz de Montellano 1996 and Brecher 1979. The Griaule material is contested and used here only as myth reported by Griaule. What this means for you: Sirius was far below the horizon at your birth. All this item gives you is a warning against taking dramatic claims at face value. 44. The Sigui The Sigui is the Dogon renewal ceremony, held about every 60 years. The last one ran from 1967 to 1973. The next is scheduled to begin in 2027 at Youga and to travel through the villages until about 2034 (bamada.net; notrenation.com; Partners Pays-Dogon 2026). What this means for you: you were born between two Siguis, and the next one starts next year. You're old enough to see the cycle turn. 45. Nommo The Nommo are the water-spirits of Griaule's account (contested). What this means for you: water again. With Bena (ocean) and Ọ̀yẹ̀kú (night), this is the third water and depth signal. Synthesis of Part IX: the Dogon material adds timing. The Sigui renewal begins in 2027.

46. Igbo Afa / Áfà, Ewe Afa, Arabic geomancy The Igbo dibia's Afa and Ewe Afa use the same 16 roots and 256 signs. The 16-figure structure is also shared with Arabic khatt al-raml geomancy and Malagasy sikidy, and scholars still argue about where it started (Maupoil 1943; Bascom 1969). What this means for you: your constructed sign would carry over into all of these.

docs.h: Part XI — Prophecy: awaited figures, tested marker by marker
docs.t: Prophecy markers Ifá doesn't promise a single messiah. Ọ̀rúnmìlà went back to heaven after his children offended him. He left the sixteen ìkín, telling them to consult those instead of waiting for him to return (Abimbọ́la 1976; ipilese.com cosmology-orunmila). The awaited figures below are tested against your markers. The markers you carry come first. 47. Ọ̀rúnmìlà's witness, the Ifá-chosen one Markers you carry: - Born on Ọjọ́ Ọ̀rúnmìlà, the day of Ifá. - Constructed Ifá sign with ire ìṣẹ́gun. - Born at day's end with Venus hidden in the Sun: "concealed light". - Odù of memory (Ìrosùn), the theme of carrying the teaching forward. Markers that can't be shown from these data: ìtẹ̀fá initiation; a real itá confirming the sign; recognition by a babaláwo lineage. 48. Odùduwa / Ọ̀rànmíyàn, the restorer-king Markers you carry: - An ancestor-first sign, Ọ̀yẹ̀kú, which is the restorer's pattern of renewing by honouring the line. - Ìrosùn: keeping the lineage's name alive. - Ire ìṣẹ́gun: victory over opposition. - Born in Ọ̀wàrà, the storm month. Markers that can't be shown: royal lineage (idílé ọba), choice by the kingmakers, and the Ifá consultation for an ọba's selection. 49. Okomfo Anokye and the Golden Stool (Akan) Markers you carry: - Kwabena, the ocean soul-day. - Born in a working stretch of the adaduanan cycle. - A destiny (nkrabea) taken from Onyame. Markers that can't be shown: priesthood (ɔkɔmfoɔ), a stool lineage. 50. The Nommo's return (Dogon, Griaule, contested) Markers you carry: - Born between Siguis, with the 2027 renewal ahead in your lifetime. - Water/ocean signals in three systems. Markers that can't be shown: Dogon initiation, Awa society membership. Synthesis of Part XI: what you carry is consistent. You were born on Ifá's own day, under a constructed sign of ancestors, memory and victory, with a hidden evening star, an ocean soul-day, and the Sigui renewal arriving within your lifetime. The traditions themselves place the deciding markers in living institutions: initiation, lineage and community recognition.

You were born on Ifá's own day, in the storm month, at dusk, while the evening star was hidden in the Sun and Jupiter was rising in the east. Your constructed Ifá sign is Ọ̀yẹ̀kú Ìrosùn (Fá: Yeku-Loso ). That means night and the ancestors, working through red camwood and memory. Ìbò gives ire ìṣẹ́gun , victory over opposition. The cowries add Òdí , the hidden thing brought out, and the kola says yes, confirm it . The Akan call you Kwabena , a soul of Tuesday and the ocean. The Dogon would place you between two Sigui renewals, with the next starting in 2027. Every one of these systems keeps coming back to depth, inheritance and coming through. Orí teaching says your character (ìwà) is the part you steer. Consult before choosing, as Afúwàpẹ́ did. Honour the line, as Ọ̀yẹ̀kú asks. Keep its memory alive, as Ìrosùn asks. Then the victory promised by ire ìṣẹ́gun comes in the second movement, after the confirmation the kola asks for. What this means for you, in one line: your West African profile is that of a keeper of memory who wins through resistance. Under the Kọ́jọ́dá convention your birth sits inside Ifá's own day. Your real Odù is still waiting for a babaláwo.

Ìpìlẹ̀ṣẹ̀ (ipilese.com): the ritual year; cosmology, time and misfortune; social time and the calendar; cosmology of Ọ̀rúnmìlà. yo.wikipedia.org, "Àgùàlà"; yoruba-scipedia (ìràwọ̀, ìràwọ̀ onírù, Òṣùmàrè, Oòrùn, Òṣùpá). Sky positions: PyEphem, computed in deep/27/compute.py.

A real birth Odù, itá or Fá Kpoli needs a living priest. The constructed cast stands in and is labelled as such. No verifiable Odù Ọdún for 1998–99. No reliably attested Yoruba names for Sirius, the Pleiades or Orion. The four-day week order and the Kọ́jọ́dá count are conventions that vary by lineage. No tradition gives a birth-derived face. IFA COMPLETE
Charles Leone — born 13 October 1998, 17:25 EDT (21:25 UT), Johnstown, Pennsylvania (40.33°N, 78.92°W). Lives in Fayetteville, North Carolina (35.05°N, 78.88°W).

docs.h: A word on respect and honesty
docs.t: The traditions in this chapter belong to living peoples. Most of them are sky calendars and navigation sciences, not horoscopes . For each item, this chapter says whether the tradition itself applies it to a person's birth or whether it is only a calendar or sky reading. Where it is only a calendar or sky reading, the "What this means for you" note is a reflective reading and is labelled as one. It is not a claim about what the tradition teaches. None of these traditions has texts that describe the faces of people born under particular stars. So no portrait faces were drawn from tradition texts , because no such texts exist. Some imagery was deliberately left out because the traditions restrict it: Haudenosaunee False Face (Gagohsa) masks Hopi katsina The sacred pipe Eagle-feather headdresses Depictions of White Buffalo Calf Woman or the Peacemaker Personal tā moko Te Kooti's flags Images of Lono's akua Computations were done in Python with ephem; the values are stored in deep/28_calc.json. At the moment of birth the Sun was 12.7° above the horizon, so this was a daylight birth , 74 minutes before sunset at 18:39 EDT. Sky dome at birth

1.1 The 30 moon nights (pō mahina) What it is: Hawaiian months count from Hilo, the first crescent. In 1998 Hilo was 21 September and the full moon fell on Hoku (5 October). This birth fell in daylight after night 22, ʻOlekūlua , a last-quarter night. Kepelino's notes say farmers disliked ʻOlekūlua for planting but it was good for torch-fishing. The alternative count gives night 21, ʻOlekūkahi. The Moon was 23.18 days old and 35% lit, and waning. Is it applied to birth? It is a calendar of work, fishing and planting. Kepelino describes the character of each night, but not as a fixed fate for a child. What this means for you (reflective): You arrived on a "not for planting, good for fishing by torchlight" night. The image is of someone who does best in the gathering phase rather than the sowing phase: finding what is already in the water, and working by a small, focused light. Hawaiian nights Moon phase Moon names 1.2 The Hawaiian month and Makahiki What it is: David Malo gives the order of the months. Makahiki opens when Makaliʻi (the Pleiades) rises at dusk. In 1998 that was about 15 November at Johnstown and about 19 November at Honolulu. Using Malo's order with that anchor, the birth lunation is Kamahoemua , about five weeks before Makahiki. Is it applied to birth? No. It is a calendar reading. What this means for you (reflective): You were born in the last working stretch before the season of peace and games. Your instinct may be to finish the harvest before you rest. Makahiki timeline 1.3 Kumulipo What it is: A cosmogonic chant in 16 wā: the 1st to 7th are Pō (darkness) and the 8th to 16th are Ao (light). It traces genealogy from coral polyps to chiefs. Is it applied to birth? It does not assign people to a wā. It is a genealogy and a cosmogony. What this means for you (reflective): A daylight birth near sunset sits symbolically at the edge between Ao and Pō. This is an image, not a teaching. Kumulipo 1.4 The PVS star compass (Nainoa Thompson) What it is: 32 houses of 11.25° each, used for wayfinding. Body House at birth Rising house Sun ʻĀina Kona (az 247.8°) Lā Malanai Moon (below horizon, alt −20.5°) Manu Hoʻolua ʻĀina Koʻolau Mercury Manu Kona ʻĀina Malanai Venus ʻĀina Kona Lā Malanai Mars ʻĀina Hoʻolua — Jupiter Lā Malanai — Saturn Noio Koʻolau — Stars visible or above the horizon at birth: Hōkūleʻa (Arcturus) at 42.0°, Lā Kona Hōkūpaʻa (Polaris) at 39.8°, ʻĀkau Rēhua (Antares) at 21.4°, Haka Kona Vega at 78.6° Altair at 46.9° Makaliʻi was below the horizon (−20.6°), in Nā Leo Koʻolau, and rises in Noio Koʻolau. Sirius and Rigel were also below the horizon. Is it applied to birth? No. The compass is for navigation. This table is a sky record, not a reading. What this means for you (reflective): Hōkūleʻa, the zenith star of Hawaiʻi and the namesake of the voyaging canoe, stood high in the west-southwest as you were born. The Sun and Venus were setting together in ʻĀina Kona. Your sky was one of homing and arrival rather than departure. Star compass Compass table Hōkūpaʻa Section synthesis (Hawaiʻi): A late-moon, harvest-end, sunset birth under Hōkūleʻa. None of these markers is assigned at birth by Hawaiian tradition. Together they give a reflective image of someone who gathers and steers home.

2.1 Maramataka What it is: Taking Whiro (the new moon) as 21 September, and using the Te Ara Ngāti Kahungunu list, night 22 is Korekore-hahani , "a fairly good day". The alternative count gives Tangaroa-ā-mua, which is good for fishing. Lists vary by iwi. Is it applied to birth? It is a working calendar. What this means for you (reflective): Your night is a moderate, steady one that leans toward Tangaroa. That echoes the Hawaiian fishing reading. Maramataka 2.2 Matariki What it is: In Rangi Mātāmua's work there are nine stars, each tied to food, water, weather or the dead. They mark the new year in midwinter. Is it applied to birth? No. It is seasonal. At your birth the cluster was below the horizon. What this means for you (reflective): You were born in the half of the year when Matariki is out of sight in the evening, which is the season of tending rather than celebrating. Matariki nine Pleiades on the birth day 2.3 Tohunga "birth-star" lore What it is: Searches found no verified Māori system that reads a destiny from the star at birth. The tohi birth rite dedicates a child through atua and whakapapa (Te Ara), not through a star. Is it applied to birth? Unverified, so it is not applied here. What this means for you: Nothing is claimed. It is better to say that than to invent something. Section synthesis (Aotearoa): Two calendar echoes, fishing and a moderate night. There is no natal star assignment.

What it is: The Pleiades are Mataliki in Tonga, Mataliʻi in Samoa and Matariʻi in Tahiti. Tahiti divides the year into Matariʻi i niʻa (abundance, from about November) and Matariʻi i raro (the lean season, from about May). Your birth falls in Matariʻi i raro. Is it applied to birth? No. It is seasonal. What this means for you (reflective): You were born late in the lean season, just before the turn to plenty. This is a pattern of patience that pays off. Section synthesis: One shared star family and one seasonal marker.

What it is: The Mohawk name for October is Kenténha, "nature getting poor". The 13-moon cycle places the Harvest Moon around this time; Seneca moon names vary by longhouse. The Pleiades are the Seven Dancers, whose position at the zenith times Midwinter. The Big Dipper is the bear and its hunters, and the bear's blood colours the autumn leaves. Is it applied to birth? It is a calendar and a set of sky stories. What this means for you (reflective): You were born exactly in red-leaf season, the time of the Bear-hunt story. It is a harvest-and-thanks month. Haudenosaunee cycle

5.1 Lenape What it is: Harrington records that the Unami annual ceremony was held between 10 and 20 October, when the leaves turned yellow. 13 October falls inside that window, which is a calendar match . The Munsee name for the October moon is Punihle-Waniipakw Niipaahum. Lenape skylore also links the Big Dipper to a bear. Is it applied to birth? No. It is a calendar. What this means for you (reflective): You were born in western Pennsylvania during the traditional Lenape thanksgiving window, a time of renewal. 5.2 Lumbee No documented Lumbee star lore was found. This is a gap, and nothing has been invented to fill it. What this means for you: You live in Fayetteville, close to Robeson County. The honest position is to learn directly from the Lumbee community rather than from books. 5.3 Cherokee What it is: The October moon is the Harvest Moon (Duninudi / Nvda Tsiyahloha), the season of the Great New Moon ceremony. Is it applied to birth? No. It is a calendar. What this means for you (reflective): For both your birthplace and your home, October is the Southeastern harvest-and-new-year season. Cherokee Residence sky Residence note: from Fayetteville, Canopus rises to about 2.3°, low in the south. From Johnstown it never rises at all. Section synthesis (Eastern Woodlands): Three independent October harvest and renewal calendars all match your birth date. This is the strongest calendar alignment in the chapter.

What it is: The Lakota October moon is Čhaŋwápekasná Wí. Goodman describes the sacred spring round, which follows the Sun from the equinox to the solstice through Aries and Triangulum, then the Pleiades, then Gemini. Your Sun in sidereal Virgo is not part of that round. Is it applied to birth? No. It is a ceremonial calendar. What this means for you (reflective): Your birth falls outside the ceremonial sky round, in the hunting and preparation season. Lakota round (approximate positions)

Each prophecy is compared with your chart marker by marker. There are no scores and no verdicts. Markers you carry are listed first. Prophecy matrix Pahana (Hopi) - Markers you carry: male (the true white brother); born in the East and living in the East (the prophecy's direction of return). - Markers not present: the red cap or red cloak; the missing corner of the stone tablet. Seventh Fire, "New People" (Anishinaabe, Benton-Banai) - Markers you carry: you belong to a generation of seekers who look back to the old ways. This marker is collective. - Markers not present: none is personal by design. The Eighth Fire is a collective choice between two roads. White Buffalo Calf Woman's return (Lakota) - Markers you carry: none of the specific markers. - Markers not present: a female figure; the birth of a white calf as the sign. Peacemaker (Haudenosaunee) - Markers you carry: symbolic only. You were born in western Pennsylvania, in lands the Seneca once claimed. - Markers not present: the specific signs of the Peacemaker's coming. Rua Kēnana, as Te Kooti's successor - Markers you carry: none of the specific markers. - Markers not present: coming from the East within Aotearoa; Mātaatua connections (Te Ara). Return of Lono (Hawaiʻi) - Markers you carry: none of the specific markers. - Markers not present: Makahiki timing. "Rainbow Warriors" - Markers you carry: none of the specific markers. - Status of the source: this comes from Willoya and Brown's 1962 tract and is documented as fakelore (Niman). It is not an authentic Native prophecy.

Across eleven traditions, the same picture keeps coming back. You were born: at the waning, gathering end of a lunar month (ʻOlekūlua / Korekore-hahani) at the harvest turn of the year (Kenténha, the Lenape ceremony, the Cherokee Harvest Moon, Čhaŋwápekasná Wí) before the Pleiades returned (before Makahiki, Matariʻi i raro) under Hōkūleʻa, the star that brings voyagers home None of these traditions assigns a fate at birth. What they offer is a seasonal identity: someone who brings things in, finishes the work, and finds the way home. The only prophecy markers you carry personally are being male and coming from the East in the Pahana account, alongside your generational share of the Seventh Fire.

No Lumbee star lore is documented. The Māori tohunga birth-star lore could not be verified. Seneca moon names vary by longhouse; one representative list was used. Night counts shift by one depending on how the evening is reckoned (ʻOlekūkahi / Tangaroa-ā-mua). Lakota constellation positions are approximate. No portrait texts exist, so no faces are drawn from tradition. POLYNESIAN-INDIGENOUS COMPLETE
